# MeTTa in Python

> Write Python, get MeTTa. Atoms are Python values, spaces are queryable
> stores, equations rewrite, and a Python function can be a MeTTa function.
> This file is how to USE the seat; the repository root's llms.txt covers the
> language and every other surface. `metta.llms()` prints that file the way
> `help()` prints, from an install as well as a checkout, and
> `python -m metta llms` is the same document from a shell. Every door named
> here exists on the object it is shown on, which `check.sh`'s `llms` lane
> checks against the live library rather than trusting this text.

## Install

```sh
pip install .            # from the repository root; the runtime is bundled
```

Or point `METTA_PATH` at a clone and import from there. You need Python 3.12+,
SWI-Prolog 9.3+, and a `janus_swi` linked against that SWI.

## First call

```python
from metta import MeTTa, S, V, G, ground, Expression, equation, rules, parse, forms

m = MeTTa()                              # binds &self
m.self.run("(= (f) 1) !(f) !(+ 1 2)")    # [[Grounded(1)], [Grounded(3)]]
m.close()                                # or `with MeTTa() as m:`
```

`m` is the CONTEXT and `m.self` its home space. The context carries the
EVALUATION doors and forwards them home, `run`, `eval`, `match`, `add`,
`define`, `op`, `transaction`, `limits`, `stats` and their kin, plus the
collection protocols, so `len(m)`, `atom in m` and `m[pattern]` read the home
space directly. Storage and introspection stay on the space: `atoms`, `type`,
`digest`, `is_function`, `arities`, `builtins` and `space_names` are reached as
`m.self.atoms()`, and asking the context for one says so rather than raising a
bare attribute error. Two contexts are independent engines' worth of state in
one process, so a library never has to own the global one.

## Atoms: four kinds, no strings

A string is text. Everything structural comes from a factory, so a rename is a
rename and the type checker can see it.

```python
S.parent(S.alice, S.bob)     # Expression (parent alice bob)
S.alice                      # Symbol
V.x                          # Variable $x
G(3.5)                       # Grounded: a Python value crossed as itself
ground(numpy_array)          # the same, explicit
Expression((S.a, S.b))       # built from a sequence
S["odd?"]                    # a head outside Python's identifier grammar
parse("(parent $x bob)")     # exactly one form
forms("(a b) (c d)")         # every top-level form, none evaluated
```

`atom.metatype` answers `Symbol`, `Variable`, `Grounded` or `Expression`.
Atoms are immutable, hashable and comparable; `a.alpha_eq(b)` is equality
modulo variable renaming, and `a.alpha(b)` BUILDS the `(=alpha a b)` term
instead of answering now. Arithmetic and bitwise operators on an atom always
BUILD: `V.x + 1` is `(+ $x 1)` and `G(2) + G(3)` is `(+ 2 3)`, not `5`. Reach
for `.value` when you meant Python's own arithmetic. Rich comparisons are the
exception and answer Python booleans in the engine's term order; `a.lt(b)` and
its siblings build the comparison term.

## Asking

```python
kb.match(S.parent(V.x, S.bob))      # -> Answers, replayable; row.x is a binding
kb[S.parent(V.x, S.bob)]            # the same, subscript spelling
kb.match(a, b)                      # a conjunction: one row per joint solution
m.eval(S.add(1, 2))                 # -> [answer, ...] flat, EAGER
m.eval(t1, t2)                      # -> [[...], [...]] one GROUP per term
m.run(source)                       # -> one answer group per `!` in the text
kb.answers(term)                    # -> Answers, the lazy chunked cursor
kb.solve(4, V.x - 1).x              # relational: runs let backwards, answers 5
kb.why(pattern)                     # why a pattern matched NOTHING
```

Return shapes are the thing you cannot guess. `match` and `answers` both hand
back `Answers`, which is lazy, replayable and chunked; `eval` is eager and
flat for ONE target but grouped for several, which is `run`'s own shape. A row
is an `Answer`: `row.x` reads a binding, and it unpacks and indexes. Answers
preserve MULTIPLICITY and do not promise order. `len(space)`,
`atom in space`, `for atom in space` and `bool(space)` (always True, a handle
is not a value that dwindles) are the container protocol; ask
`bool(space.match(p))` when the question is emptiness.

## Defining: two doors, and the price of each

```python
@m.define                      # LOWERED: the body BECOMES equations
def double(x):
    return fn.mul(x, 2)        # explicit engine relation

@m.op(effect="oracleIO")       # CALLED: the engine calls into Python
def fetch(url): ...

m.define(prolog=source, name="p-sum")   # a Prolog predicate as the function
equation(S.f(V.x)).to(V.x + 1)          # one equation, built
rules(...)                              # a generator yielding equations
```

Measured per call on the extension-cost workload (`python -m
benchmarks.extension_cost` from `extensions/python`), which subtracts the
driver's own cost so a row is the marginal cost of one call:

| door | inferences/call | microseconds/call |
|---|---|---|
| translator rule (a macro) | 0.00 | below the driver |
| C foreign predicate | 1.00 | 0.02 |
| Prolog grounded predicate | 2.00 | 0.03 |
| an ordinary MeTTa function | 3.00 | 0.06 |
| `@m.define`, annotated | 3.00 | 0.07 |
| `m.op`, `transport="raw"` | 12.00 | 1.15 |
| `m.op`, encoded | 20.00 | 4.29 |
| `@m.define`, no annotations | 28.00 | 5.47 |

Read the two columns differently. The inference column is deterministic, three
identical samples per tier across two whole runs on 2026-09-06, and it is what
the benchmark's committed baseline gates. The microsecond column came from the
same run at load average 12, so take it for the magnitude of the crossing and
not as a pin.

The two `@m.define` rows are the same door and nine times apart. An annotated
body compiles to a native operator and costs what an ordinary MeTTa function
costs; without annotations the operators go through Python's live protocol at
application time, which is a host crossing per operation. Annotate a compiled
body you care about the cost of.

So reach for `@m.define` when the body is expressible as MeTTa, and `m.op`
when it must stay Python: it touches the network, holds a file, or calls a
library you are not going to re-express. A called operation must DECLARE its
effect class, because the engine cannot see inside it, and only a
`pureStructural` one is cached without being asked. A written `!(memoize f)`,
`!(memoize-exact f)`, `!(tabled (f $x))` or `(cache f force)` is honoured
whatever the class says.

The ordered `EffectClass` members are: `pureStructural`, `readOnlyLookup`,
`nondeterministicReadOnly`, `writesState`, `oracleIO`. Those five are what
`effect=` takes and the names reflection answers with; there are no
shorthands, and a spelling outside the five is refused by name. Three retired
inputs still map in, `immutable`, `stable` and `volatile`, reaching
`pureStructural`, `readOnlyLookup` and `oracleIO`. Registering a generator
lifts the class to at least `nondeterministicReadOnly` by itself.

## What a compiled BODY may say

There is no unsupported-construct list. `try`/`except`/`else`/`finally` and
`raise` compile onto the engine's error algebra, so `except ValueError as e`
matches live classes by identity and inheritance and `str(e)` reads as
Python's; dict and set literals are
`lib_dict` spaces, so `d[k]`, `k in d`, `d[k] = v`, `del d[k]`, `len(d)` and
the view methods all reach the library's vocabulary; comprehensions,
generators (`yield` is nondeterminism, one answer per yield), `match`,
walrus, `global`, and `type X = T` all compile.

Tuple and list assignment bind engine expression patterns; a shape mismatch
answers nothing. Generator `match` arms retain their captures in subsequent
yields. `case S.Empty` selects a subject that produced no answers.

`list(generator())` gathers a known compiled generator's answers into one
engine expression. `list(range(n))` returns a host list. If a deterministic
call could mean either returned data or collected answers, use `collapse(...)`
to collect answers, or bind the returned data before calling `list`.
`type(value)` queries the engine metatype after evaluating its operand;
`py(type(value))` requests the Python class. `typing.overload` stubs on one
compiled definition publish all distinct signatures with its fixed arity.

Generic operators (`+`, comparisons, bitwise operations, unary operations,
and builtins such as `sum`) invoke Python's live protocol at application
time. That preserves reflected methods and result species, and is classified
`oracleIO` because a dunder can have host effects. Use `fn.add`, `fn.lt`,
`fn.bit_and`, `fn.floor_div`, and sibling `fn` names when the body means an
engine relation that should remain pure, matchable, or reversible.

Anything else odd becomes a visible host island inside the equation, run per
application and never at decoration time, which is what `py(...)` spells
explicitly. A refusal cites its ground in one of the two languages rather
than a house rule, and renders the file, function, line and an exact caret.

One trap worth knowing: Python's `/` is true division, so a compiled `n / 2`
faithfully answers a float. The engine's own divisions are `fn.truediv(a, b)`
and `fn.floor_div(a, b)`.

## What a VALUE crosses as, a different choice

`py-atom` takes the image as an argument, independent of the door above: a
lowered body can still take an opaque argument.

```python
m.run('!(py-atom numpy.absolute Grounded)')     # opaque: the live reference
m.run('!(py-atom numpy.absolute Expression)')   # transparent: a snapshot
```

Transparent means translated into MeTTa structure. Opaque means carried whole
as a blob the engine holds and does not read, which keeps host identity and
skips a translation you may not want. Neither is the lesser one. An iterator
is always opaque, because measuring one drains it.

## Spaces

```python
kb = m.space(S.kb)          # a handle; naming one does not create it
kb = m.space()              # fresh and anonymous; a context manager that drops
kb += S.parent(S.alice, S.bob)
kb += [(S.Edge, 1, 2), (S.Edge, 2, 3)]   # a fact STREAM: two atoms
kb += (S.Edge, 1, 2)                      # a tuple of scalars: ONE atom
```

Removal has three doors and they differ in how much they take and what they
say about absence:

```python
kb.remove(atom)          # ONE occurrence, answers True/False
kb.remove(a, b, c)       # the same grain, batched, answers how many were found
kb -= atom               # ONE occurrence, no verdict: += and -= are inverses
del kb[pattern]          # the DRAIN: every unifying occurrence, one crossing
                         # raises KeyError when nothing matched
```

`-=` is Python's in-place difference over a MULTISET, and Python's multiset is
`collections.Counter`, whose `-=` subtracts the multiplicity given rather than
clearing the key. MeTTa spells the pair `subtract-atom` and `remove-atom`.

```python
kb.transfer(x, y, to=other)   # move one occurrence each, one transaction
kb |= other                   # bulk merge; a space is a multiset
kb.clear(); kb.drop()         # empty it; end its whole life and free the name
kb.copy(); kb.digest()        # clone contents; content identity
kb.source()                   # directly stored program as loadable MeTTa
kb.save("program.metta")      # writes exactly kb.source()
kb.consumption("repeated")    # writes (source <space> repeated) in the catalog
```

`python -m metta convert program.py [-o out.metta]` imports the module against
a fresh space and prints or writes its declarations as loadable MeTTa source.

`metta.spaces` composes without copying: `union(*spaces)` reads a set as one,
`overlay(front, back)` reads both and writes to the front, `readonly(s)`
refuses writes by capability, `mapped(s, shape)` is a shape view from one
declaration, `view(obj)` presents a live Python object as a space, and
`diff(a, b)` says HOW two spaces differ where `digest()` only says THAT they
do. `metta.foreign` is the other direction: implement `Matcher`/`Adder`/
`Remover` and register any backend as a space. `metta.remote` puts one across
a process boundary, `metta.tables` derives one from a table.

## The three seams anything plugs into

It is a KERNEL because the point is what plugs into it, and a thing you want
to use lands on one of three seams rather than needing a fork.

**Lower it.** Host code BECOMES equations: `@m.define` compiles a Python body
into MeTTa the engine reads, specialises and matches on, and a translator rule
adds syntax that costs nothing at run time.

**Extend it.** The engine CALLS your code: `m.op`, `m.register_prolog`,
`m.register_foreign_library` and a reader token class each make a host
callable or literal into an ordinary MeTTa one, priced 1 to 20 inferences a
call by how far the value travels, in the table above.

**Back it.** The atoms LIVE elsewhere: a space is an interface, so SQLite,
DuckDB, NetworkX, a live Python object, another process or a MORK store can
BE a space, and a query against one joins with a native one.

The third is the one people underestimate. A table-backed space is one
declaration, not a wrapper:

```python
kb = m.self                     # both take a SPACE, not the context
tables.declare(kb, "&crm", "(bridge (edge $a $b) (row edges (a $a) (b $b)))")
provider = TableBridge.from_context(kb, "&crm", sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))
metta.attach("&crm", provider)  # the name is now a queryable space
```

Every provider operation derives from that one declaration, both directions:
a match becomes a WHERE, a repeated variable becomes `WHERE a = b`, `take`
pushes down a LIMIT, an add becomes an INSERT, and the declaration is itself
knowledge a program can query. `metta.foreign` is the hand-written form of
the same seam, `metta.remote` puts a space in another process, and
`metta.spaces.view` presents a live Python object as one.

`extensions/python/examples/language-feature-examples/` is 224 runnable
programs, each mirroring one MeTTa example's path. The `twins` REPORT lane
runs each against the MeTTa it mirrors and prints what a twin cannot yet say;
an example without a twin is a backlog row rather than a gap in the corpus.
They are the reference for idiomatic code on this surface.

## Types, and checking them

```python
m += typed(S.f, arrow(S.Number, S.Number))   # (: f (-> Number Number))
kb.type(atom)                                 # the first get-type answer
kb.cast(value, S.Number)                      # runtime cast on the engine's rules
```

Annotations on a `@m.define` become the declaration, and a local annotation
becomes an enforceable in-place claim.

## Concurrency, transactions, bounds

```python
from metta import spawn, par_map, race, channel, parallel
future = spawn(term)          # a FutureSpace; wait(), settled(), cancel()
par_map(fn, items); race(a, b); channel()
m.transaction(term)           # all-or-nothing; rollback delivers no events
with m.limits(inferences=10_000, timeout=1.0): ...
with m.speculate(): ...       # run and discard
```

An abandoned future warns rather than spinning silently.

## Seeing what happened

```python
with m.stats() as s: ...      # s.inferences (deterministic), cputime, walltime
m.trace(term)                 # the reduction trace; .stopped names the bound that cut it
m.trace(term, filter=[S.f])   # only the named functions are recorded
with m.debug(term, on=[S.f]) as d:  # breakpoints; the loop body is the suspension
m.self.derivation(term)       # the proof tree; premises and effects execute
m.self.speculative()          # scope a derivation to discard engine writes
m.self.lint()                 # diagnostics over declarations, equations, calls
m.self.effect_plan(term)      # named operations and joined effect, without execution
m.self.subscribe(pattern, cb, on="both")   # a standing query; on= add/remove/both
m.self.watch(pattern)         # the iterator face of the same
```

Inferences are deterministic and wall clock is not; gate on the former.

## The rest of the library, by module

`metta.aio` is the same engine without blocking an event loop (`AsyncMeTTa`).
`metta.arrays` crosses arrays for anything speaking the buffer standard.
`metta.structures` has the stores worth having with MeTTa's semantics at
Python speed: `AlphaSet`, `PatternMap`, `MatchIndex`, `LiveView`,
`ClosureView`, `TabledMap`. `metta.events` is the public event stream and
`metta.subscribe` its two delivery models. `metta.convert` registers two-way
conversions, `metta.casting` runtime casts, `metta.integrate` is the
interface a library implements to work deeply with the engine, `metta.paths`
builds cycle-safe lazy structural paths, `metta.manifest` makes deployment
knowledge (`metta.boot(path)` assembles an app), `metta.derivation` and
`metta.trace` reify proofs and reductions, `metta.lint` reports diagnostics,
and `metta.testing` ships hypothesis strategies for property-testing code
built on this surface.

`m += lib.x` imports one of the engine's 38 MeTTa libraries through the write
door, because a library IS knowledge and the receiver is the target space.

## When it refuses

Every refusal is typed and carries machine-readable parts beside the message:
`MettaError` is the base (with `atom`, `space`, `operation`, `capability`,
`ground`), `CompileError` names the construct and renders a caret, and
`SpaceCapabilityError` names the space, operation and missing capability.
An error has two readings in MeTTa. An `(Error ...)` written literally, or an
answer bound before its next call, is data and can be compared or inspected.
A strict argument whose evaluation produces an `(Error ...)` instead finishes
the enclosing call with that error unchanged. Use `if-error`,
`return-on-error`, or an explicit `let` binding before treating the answer as
data; a parameter declared `Atom` receives its written argument without
evaluating it.

## The ladder, and it never shrinks

Python here, MeTTa source through `run`/`parse`, Prolog through
`m.register_prolog(source=..., path=..., names=...)`, and C through
`m.register_foreign_library(path, entry=, names=)`. Each rung is reachable
from the one above, and the fast path is the idiomatic one.

## Where to read next

- `website/tutorials/` teaches the language from Python, one idea at a time.
- `website/guide/` is task-oriented: queries, definitions, spaces, threads.
- `website/reference/` reproduces every public module's exact signatures.
- `extensions/python/examples/` are runnable programs that print checked claims.
